label: AQ 0045
title: The penalty that kept the reward honest

questions.q: If the penalty protects us, why not make β large?
questions.a: InstructGPT's human ratings (PPO with pretraining data mixed in) were poor at β = 2 as at β = 0, with the best around 0.01 to 0.02. Our reasoning for why: too large a β holds the policy near the SFT model, leaving RL little room to improve it.

teach.title: How it works: what the penalty is, then how to set it

questions.q: How does DPO deal with the same issue?
questions.a: DPO solves the same KL-constrained objective directly from preference pairs, so β sits inside its loss rather than in a separate penalty. A larger β keeps the model closer to the reference; a smaller one lets it drift further.

teach.title: How it works: what the penalty is, then how to set it

questions.q: The score keeps climbing. How do you spot reward hacking?
questions.a: Track a second score the policy isn't trained on, such as human ratings or a held-out judge. Gao et al. found such a score (a 6B reward model standing in for people) rises and then falls as KL grows, while the trained-on score keeps rising. Keeping the checkpoint where the second score peaks is our suggestion.

teach.title: How it works: what the penalty is, then how to set it

questions.q: In InstructGPT's RLHF, what is subtracted from the reward model's score, and with what β?
questions.a: β times the log of the policy's probability over the SFT model's, a per-token KL penalty, with β = 0.02.

teach.title: How it works: what the penalty is, then how to set it

questions.q: What did Ziegler et al. get when they tuned GPT-2 against a stand-in sentiment classifier with no KL penalty?
questions.a: Gibberish of repeated words (“These These These… easily easily easily”), which the classifier still scored at about +8.0, 99.97% positive.

questions.q: Why isn't the safest choice for β simply a very large value?
questions.a: InstructGPT's human ratings (PPO with pretraining data mixed in) were poor at β = 2 as well as at β = 0, best around 0.01 to 0.02. Our reasoning: a large β holds the policy near the SFT model, leaving training little room to improve it.
